solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Liberal dons tolerate American state

indicators.note: to don is to put on, as a garment, so one piece wears another around it

blocks.note: to bear something is to put up with it
L is the standard abbreviation for Liberal
US is short for United States, hence American

explanation.surface: Broad-minded academics put up with an American state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American state' looks like the definition, but 'American' only supplies US; the state is an ex-Soviet country in eastern Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: Belarus is a sovereign country, and a nation is commonly called a state.

clue.text: Saw Times superior to Express

indicators.note: in a down clue, being superior means sitting higher, so this piece comes above the next

blocks.note: as in three by four, meaning three times four
to express something is to word it

explanation.surface: A boast that The Times newspaper outranks the Daily Express.
explanation.walkthrough: Times and Express read as rival newspapers; 'superior to' simply puts one piece on top of the other in the down grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old saying or proverb, and a byword is a proverbial phrase too.

clue.text: British measure time fielder has to catch

indicators.note: catching something means holding it, so one piece takes another inside

blocks.note: long on is a cricket fielding position near the boundary behind the bowler
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator notes that a British fielder has time to take a catch.
explanation.walkthrough: Long on is a cricket position, deep on the leg side behind the bowler; T slips between its two words.
explanation.definitionFit: The long ton is the imperial unit of weight of 2,240 pounds used in Britain.

clue.text: Spirited mum collects one, on coming first

indicators.note: to collect is to gather in, so one piece takes another inside it
something coming first is placed at the front of the rest

blocks.note: RE means on or about, as in business letters
to keep mum is to stay quiet
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A lively mother collects someone, arriving ahead of the others.
explanation.walkthrough: Mum is not a mother but the adjective meaning quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: A resilient person bounces back with plenty of spirit, so the two adjectives overlap in meaning.

clue.text: Search on the ground for brick, in last resort

indicators.note: ground things are crushed and broken up, so these letters are reduced and remixed

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Hunting on the ground for a building brick as a last resort.
explanation.walkthrough: A brick, in informal British use, is a dependable person; here the definition is that sense, qualified by 'in last resort'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheet anchor was a large spare anchor used in emergencies, figuratively a person or thing relied on when all else fails.

clue.text: Judge of mince pies providing some humour

blocks.note: J is the abbreviation for judge
mince pies is rhyming slang for eyes, and ocular means of the eyes

explanation.surface: Someone judging a mince pie contest makes it rather comic.
explanation.walkthrough: Mince pies are small Christmas pastries in Britain, and in cockney rhyming slang they stand for eyes.
explanation.definitionFit: Jocular describes remarks meant in jest, so something jocular supplies a bit of amusement.

clue.text: Old invader’s unfinished project

indicators.note: something unfinished lacks its end, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a member of a Germanic people who invaded Britain in the fifth century

explanation.surface: An ancient invader's scheme was left incomplete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Project' reads as a noun, a scheme, but it is the verb meaning to stick out.
explanation.definitionFit: To jut is to stick out beyond a surface, which is what projecting means as a verb.

clue.text: Small portion of broccoli causing complaint

indicators.note: a small portion is a piece taken from within, so the letters sit inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Eating just a little broccoli gives someone a stomach upset.
explanation.walkthrough: Complaint here is the medical sense, an ailment, not a grumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint can mean an illness or disorder, and colic is a painful abdominal disorder.

clue.text: Gross politician, one visiting boozer

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone else's place, so pieces go inside another

blocks.note: a Member of Parliament
I is the Roman numeral one
a lush is a heavy drinker

explanation.surface: A disgusting politician drops into the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a boozer is also a pub, which the surface suggests; here it is a drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: Gross in the sense of heavy, coarse and clumsy matches lumpish, meaning bulky and oafish.

clue.text: Newton, say, engrossed in study, finally forgave dissident

indicators.note: someone engrossed is absorbed, so pieces sit deep inside another
finally points to the very end of a word, keeping only its last letter

blocks.note: to read a subject is to study it
N is the symbol for the newton, the unit of force
e.g. means for example
its closing letter

explanation.surface: Isaac Newton, absorbed in his work, eventually pardoned a rebel.
explanation.walkthrough: Newton looks like the scientist, but it is the unit of force, symbol N, and 'say' is e.g.
explanation.definitionFit: A renegade deserts a cause or party, much as a dissident breaks with the official line.

clue.text: Exposed snakes showed signs of distress

blocks.note: a path that snakes winds
cried

explanation.surface: Uncovered snakes looked upset.
explanation.walkthrough: Snakes is the verb, meaning follows a twisting course, not the reptiles.
explanation.definitionFit: A windswept place is open to the full force of gales, so it is exposed.

clue.text: Dud shade

blocks.note: first meaning: something that fails or does not work
second meaning: a pale yellow colour

explanation.walkthrough: Both words are nouns: a lemon is slang for a faulty product, and also the name of a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A defective car bought secondhand is called a lemon, and lemon is also a named pale yellow colour.

clue.text: Carnivore heading for lair put on speed

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its top, meaning its opening letter
in an across clue, putting one thing on another means adding it alongside

blocks.note: rate is pace or speed
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A meat-eater heading for its den speeds up.
explanation.walkthrough: The ratel is the honey badger of Africa and Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: The ratel, or honey badger, is a flesh-eating mammal, so it is an example of a carnivore.

clue.text: Architect ultimately devising natural alternative to tiles

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the closing letter is kept

blocks.note: its closing letter
to hatch a plan is to devise it

explanation.surface: An architect finally designs a roof of natural materials instead of tiles.
explanation.walkthrough: Devising suggests designing, but it is hatching, as in hatching a plot; the definition describes straw or reed roofing.
explanation.definitionFit: Straw or reed roofing material laid on a roof is a plant-based covering used instead of slate or clay.

clue.text: Severe stress some of Proust’s characters may be under?

definitions.text: some of Proust’s characters may be under?

blocks.note: an acute pain is a severe one
an accent is emphasis or stress on a syllable

explanation.surface: Proust's fictional people may suffer from great strain.
explanation.walkthrough: Characters are letters, not people in a novel: French words such as those Proust wrote carry marks over some vowels.
explanation.definitionFit: The rising diagonal mark over an e in French is placed above written letters, so letters sit under it.

clue.text: Not getting enough — hundred euros in change

indicators.note: to change something is to alter it, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is short-changed, receiving a hundred euros in coins but not enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In change' reads as coins, but 'in' belongs to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Undernourished people lack adequate food, so they are short of the nutrition they need.

clue.text: Bias current medic’s shown facing a cut in surgery

blocks.note: I is the symbol for electric current
MB is a Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor
taken as written
to lance a boil is to cut it open

explanation.surface: A doctor with a current bias is shown facing a cutback in surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: Current is the electrical quantity, whose symbol is I.
explanation.definitionFit: A bias tilts things one way, so it amounts to a lack of balance or even-handedness.

clue.text: Offer short clue that’s defective but compelling

indicators.note: something short is cut off early, so the last letter goes
something defective is faulty and out of order, so letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: A crossword setter offers a brief clue that is flawed yet gripping.
explanation.walkthrough: Short trims one word only, and defective then shuffles all eight surviving letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A compelling argument has strong persuasive power, just as a forceful one does.

clue.text: Banned athlete sadly submits, the worse for wear

indicators.note: things going sadly are going badly wrong, so letters fall out of order

blocks.note: out as in ruled out or excluded
taken as written
to bow to someone is to submit

explanation.surface: A suspended athlete unhappily gives in, looking ragged.
explanation.walkthrough: Banned gives OUT, as a player ruled out; only the athlete's letters are shuffled, and the bows are added after.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes worn through at the joints of the sleeves suggest shabbiness, so the idiom means shabby or worn.

clue.text: Most banal customs dividing races

indicators.note: to divide something is to split it apart, with a piece inserted in between

blocks.note: the TT races are motorcycle races on the Isle of Man
rites are ceremonial customs

explanation.surface: The dullest traditions separate the ethnic groups.
explanation.walkthrough: Races suggests peoples, but it is TT, the Tourist Trophy motorcycle races on the Isle of Man.
explanation.definitionFit: Trite means overused and unoriginal, and its superlative is the most banal of all.

clue.text: Ne’er-do-well king borne in litter by learner

indicators.note: carried inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: litter is rubbish
R is short for rex, king
L is the learner-driver plate

explanation.surface: A worthless monarch is carried in a sedan chair alongside a novice.
explanation.walkthrough: Litter hints at a carried couch for royalty, but it means rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: A wastrel squanders their life and money, which is exactly what a good-for-nothing does.

clue.text: The last place, perhaps, to introduce unknown stars

indicators.note: introducing something brings it in, so one piece is inserted into another

blocks.note: Hades, the underworld, is one's final resting place; perhaps marks it as an example
y is a mathematical unknown

explanation.surface: An obscure spot is the final place for launching little-known celebrities.
explanation.walkthrough: The stars look like celebrities, but they are real ones; the unknown is the algebraic y.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hyades are an open cluster of stars in the constellation Taurus.

clue.text: Gallant vicar with child briefly out of hand

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the last letter is lost
things out of hand are out of control, so letters run wild

blocks.note: taken as written
the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: A courteous clergyman whose child is briefly unruly.
explanation.walkthrough: Gallant is the definition at the front; the child loses its last letter before joining the vicar in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Gallant behaviour is courteous and brave, the ideals of the medieval knightly code.

clue.text: Joint from an ungulate served up

indicators.note: in a down clue, sending something up makes it read bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
an elk is a hoofed mammal

explanation.surface: A joint of meat from a hoofed animal is brought to the table.
explanation.walkthrough: Joint suggests a roast, but it is the body part.
explanation.definitionFit: The ankle is the hinge connecting the foot and leg, one of the body's joints.

clue.text: Vigorous, if in need of practice, having changed sides

indicators.note: switching sides means swapping right for left, one letter for another

blocks.note: skills out of practice become rusty

explanation.surface: A strong player, if short of practice, has swapped teams.
explanation.walkthrough: Sides are R for right and L for left; the R at the front becomes L.
explanation.definitionFit: Lusty means full of health and energy, a close synonym of vigorous.

clue.text: Oddly for each thousand you get a mutant

indicators.note: oddly points to the odd-numbered positions, first, third and so on

blocks.note: its first and third letters
its first and third letters
K stands for a thousand

explanation.surface: Strangely, every thousand births produce a mutation.
explanation.walkthrough: Oddly applies to each of the two short words separately, taking their first and third letters; K for thousand comes from kilo.
explanation.definitionFit: A freak of nature is an abnormal creature, as a mutant is.

clue.text: Thirsting for blood, as was McCarthy, mostly?

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: Senator Joseph McCarthy saw communists, reds, everywhere in 1950s America

explanation.surface: A bloodthirsty mood, like the anti-communist witch-hunter's.
explanation.walkthrough: McCarthy famously found communists under every bed; dropping the plural's last letter leaves the idiom for rage.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone seeing red is furiously angry, in a violent mood that could be called bloodthirsty.

clue.text: Backward throw

blocks.note: first meaning: bashful, slow to come forward
second meaning: to toss or fling

explanation.walkthrough: Backward looks like a reversal signal, but here it means diffident.
explanation.definitionFit: A reserved person is described as shy or backward, and to shy a stone is to fling it.

clue.text: Large mammal gets last of prey — it’s a chancy business

indicators.note: the last of a word is its closing letter

blocks.note: L is the size label for large
an otter is a mammal
its closing letter

explanation.surface: A big animal catches the last of its prey in a hunt that depends on luck.
explanation.walkthrough: Large mammal reads as one phrase, but large only supplies L, as on clothing labels.
explanation.definitionFit: A lottery is a draw decided purely by luck, so any risky affair can be called one.

clue.text: Return of stone edging even less healthy for plant support

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the letters read right to left
an edging runs round the border, so it surrounds whatever lies within

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight
more ill

explanation.surface: A gardener brings back stone edging for an even sicklier climbing plant.
explanation.walkthrough: ST is the abbreviation for the stone, a British weight of fourteen pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A trellis is a lattice framework on which climbing plants grow, so it holds them up.
